name: Stem cell hair therapy
lead: Stem cell hair therapy is an umbrella term for treatments that inject or apply cells, or products derived from cells, to the scalp in order to slow hair loss or promote regrowth. Variants include adipose-derived (fat) stem cell preparations, stromal vascular fraction, cells cultured from a patient's own hair follicles, donor mesenchymal stem cells, and cell-conditioned extracts or secretomes. [3][7][1][8]

Clinics that offer such procedures say the cells release growth factors that reawaken miniaturised follicles. Researchers are testing these ideas in small registered trials, many of them early phase or without a control comparison. [3][7][8] Wikipedia notes that as of 2024 the only FDA-approved stem-cell therapy is hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, and that hundreds of US clinics have sold mostly unproven stem-cell treatments, with the FDA and FTC taking enforcement action against some. [11]
infobox: Adipose tissue, own hair follicle cells, donor mesenchymal cells
Androgenetic alopecia; alopecia areata in some trials
No stem-cell hair treatment approved in the US (per Wikipedia, only HSCT is approved) [11]

paras: The label covers several different procedures. Some use a patient's own fat, processed into stromal vascular fraction or cultured adipose-derived cells; some multiply mesenchymal cells taken from the patient's hair follicles; others use donor cells or cell-free extracts from donor cell cultures. [7][3][8][1] Related but distinct entries on this wiki cover exosomes and hair cloning (culturing follicle-forming cells for implantation).

Small trials have been registered for stem-cell-based hair treatment, though no published results from them are cited in this article. A completed 38-person study tested an allogeneic adipose stem cell component extract in androgenetic alopecia [1]. A completed study of 50 people tested autologous hair-follicle-derived mesenchymal stem cell suspension [3], and a completed phase 2 study of 22 people tested adipose-derived stem cells combined with platelet-rich plasma [7].

Other registrations include a 70-person phase 1/2 study of allogeneic mesenchymal stem cells for androgenetic alopecia [8], a phase 4 comparison of adipose-derived stem cells versus platelet-rich plasma after follicular unit extraction (n=40) [9], a study of 'Stem Cell Educator' therapy in alopecia areata (n=20) [5], a 60-person regeneration study in androgenetic alopecia [6], and a trial of umbilical cord stem cell exosomes (n=50) [10]. Wikipedia describes one case report of improved hair density after combined CD34+ and umbilical cord stem cell treatment, and cautions that a single case offers limited evidence. [11] Registration on ClinicalTrials.gov does not mean a study has been reviewed or approved. [11]

Wikipedia reports that clinics selling unapproved stem-cell treatments typically charge $10,000 to $20,000, that the FTC in 2018 required some to pay refunds for unsubstantiated claims, and that the FDA has sued some firms over unapproved adipose stem cell products. [11] It also reports infections in at least 20 US patients after cord-blood products marketed as stem-cell treatments in 2021. [11] These reports concern stem-cell clinics generally rather than hair treatment specifically.

card.summary: Clinic injections of fat-derived or follicle-derived cells for hair regrowth; small trials registered, no approved product.
card.aka: Adipose stem cell hair treatment, SVF hair restoration
card.note: Wikipedia reports regulator action against unapproved stem-cell clinics; costs often run $10,000+.

quick.overview:
Stem cell hair therapy covers procedures that place cells or cell-derived products into the scalp to counter hair loss. Sources include a patient's fat, hair follicle cells or donor mesenchymal cells.

Small trials are registered, but no published results are cited here and no such treatment is FDA-approved for hair loss.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say the cells secrete growth factors that stimulate dormant follicles. In the cited sources this is a proposed mechanism under study in early trials.
quick.risks: Wikipedia reports FDA and FTC action against clinics selling unapproved stem-cell treatments, and serious infections after some cell products in 2021 (not hair-specific). Costs are commonly high and insurance typically does not cover them.
